## Research Question

Monitoring Near-Earth Objects (NEOs) is critical for planetary defense and assessing potential impact risks to Earth. Our project is investigating what orbital and physical characteristics of an asteroid defined as an NEO could make it potentially hazardous. NASA already has a strict, predefined definition for what makes an asteroid potentially hazardous to Earth - an NEO must satisfy both the criteria: having an absolute magnitude less than 22 (a variable that is inversly proportional to the estimated diameter of an asteroid, which cannot be found directly by physical measurement), and the minimum orbit intersection distance (MOID) with Earth be less than 0.05 AU We want to produce two models; one that aims to replicate NASA's definitions, including the variables MOID and diameter and another which doesn't include variables included in NASA's defintions, so they don't mathematically dominate the model, letting us investigate which underlying orbital and kinematic features actually drive hazard risk.

### Model Development and Preliminary Results (Kate first draft)

We developed two logistic regression models to investigate which asteroid characteristics are most useful for predicting whether an asteroid is potentially hazardous.

Both models were developed using backward feature selection, starting with an initial set of 20 candidate predictors. For the Model Independent From NASA Сriteria (Independent Model), three parameters associated with NASA's existing hazard assessment approach were excluded before feature selection, leaving 17 candidate predictors. The selection procedure then iteratively removed predictors when doing so improved the mean ROC-AUC obtained through five-fold cross-validation.

As a result, the Full Model retained 15 predictors, while the Independent Model retained 14 predictors. The purpose of this comparison is to investigate whether asteroid hazard status can be predicted effectively using alternative characteristics, without relying directly on NASA's existing criteria.

Both models were trained using the training dataset. Their performance was evaluated using ROC-AUC, with five-fold cross-validation used during feature selection.

The cross-validation results for the Independent Model were relatively consistent across the five folds, with a mean ROC-AUC of 0.882. Its ROC-AUC on the training dataset was 0.884, suggesting consistent performance during cross-validation and training.

However, the test results were unexpectedly high. Both models achieved a ROC-AUC of approximately 0.988, despite having different predictors and substantially different predicted probabilities. This discrepancy between cross-validation and test performance requires further investigation.

Our preliminary analysis also showed that NASA's two main hazard assessment criteria, minimum orbit intersection distance and absolute magnitude, almost perfectly reproduce the hazard classification in our dataset, with only 10 disagreements among 4,981 test observations. This suggests that the target variable is strongly associated with these criteria and may also be predictable from other, correlated orbital characteristics.

In the next stage, we will investigate the unexpectedly high test ROC-AUC, check for missing data and differences between the training and test datasets, and verify that the evaluation procedure is consistent. We will then reassess the models' performance and determine how reliably the Independent Model can predict asteroid hazard status without directly using NASA's criteria.
